inline.s: [Polishing medicine] the medicine for polishing a mirror, a chemical substance used in ancient times to grind and polish the surface of a bronze mirror.

Someone asks: Above it was said that the Dharma-realm is of a single mark and that the Buddha-body is not two. Why, then, do we not only single-mindedly recollect true thusness, but also rely upon studying and practicing the manifold wholesome dharmas? I answer: This is like a great mani jewel, whose essence is bright and pure yet harbors the filth of ore and dross. If a person, though he recollects the jewel-nature, does not by skillful means grind and polish it in every way, he will never attain its purity. Because the defilement is immeasurable and pervades all dharmas, therefore he cultivates every wholesome practice.

Question: Above it was said that the Dharma-realm is of a single mark and that the Buddha-body is not two. Why should we not only single-mindedly recollect true thusness, but still need to rely on cultivating the manifold wholesome practices? Answer: This is like a great mani jewel — although its essence is bright and pure, it is covered by the filth and dross of the ore. If there is a person who, though he constantly recollects the bright, pure essence of the jewel, does not use skillful means to polish and repair it, he will in the end never obtain the bright and pure jewel. Because the defilement of the mind is immeasurable and pervades all dharmas, therefore one must cultivate every wholesome practice.

Thus the dharma-nature of true thusness is originally empty and pure, and yet it has immeasurable afflictions and stains. If a person, though he recollects true thusness, does not by skillful means apply various kinds of permeating cultivation, he likewise will never attain purity; because the defilement is immeasurable and pervades all dharmas. Therefore he cultivates all wholesome practices as an antidote; for if a person cultivates all wholesome dharmas, he will naturally return and accord with the dharma of true thusness.

Thus the dharma-nature of true thusness is originally empty and pure, and yet it has immeasurable afflictions and stains. If there is a person who, though he constantly recollects true thusness, does not use skillful means to apply various kinds of permeating cultivation, true thusness will also not become empty and pure — this is because the defilement is immeasurable and pervades all dharmas. Therefore one must cultivate all wholesome practices as an antidote. For if one cultivates all wholesome dharmas, one will naturally return and accord with the dharma of true thusness.

According to what is discussed here, making the deluded mind come to rest and cease is the primary practice, and cultivating the various wholesome dharmas is the auxiliary practice. When one cultivates wholesome deeds, one should be in accord with the mind of non-attachment and not grasp at cause and effect. If one grasps at cause and effect, one falls into the retribution of the human and heavenly realms of the ordinary person, and will find it hard to realize true thusness or transcend birth and death. If one is in accord with the mind of non-attachment, this is the essential art of realizing true thusness and transcending birth and death, and one simultaneously attains vast merit and virtue. The Diamond Prajna Sutra says: 'Subhuti, a bodhisattva who practices giving without being attached to marks — that merit is inexpressible.'

According to what is discussed here, one should take making the deluded mind come to rest and cease as the primary practice and cultivating the various wholesome dharmas as the auxiliary practice. When one cultivates wholesome deeds, one should be in accord with the mind of non-attachment and not grasp at cause and effect. If one grasps at cause and effect, one falls into the retribution of the human and heavenly realms of ordinary beings, and will find it hard to realize true thusness or transcend birth and death. If one cultivates wholesome deeds in accord with the mind of non-attachment, this is the essential art of realizing true thusness and transcending birth and death, and one simultaneously attains vast merit and virtue. The Diamond Sutra says: 'Subhuti, a bodhisattva who practices giving without being attached to marks — that merit is inexpressible.'

Now I see that there are people who study and practice: as soon as they learn that there is an original Buddha-nature, they presume upon their innate, untainted nature and do not practice the manifold wholesome deeds. Not only do they fail to reach the true mind, they even turn instead toward indolence. They cannot even escape the evil destinies, let alone transcend birth and death? This view is a great error!

Now I see that there are people who study and practice: as soon as they learn that there is an original Buddha-nature, they presume that since they are already Buddhas, why need they practice the manifold wholesome deeds. They not only fail to reach the realm of the true mind, they also become indolent and lazy. In this way, they cannot even avoid the evil destinies, let alone wish to transcend birth and death? Therefore, this view that one need not cultivate wholesome deeds is utterly and hopelessly wrong! (The Song of Realizing the Way says: 'Careless and haughty, one invites calamity and disaster!')

blocks.text: 12. The Merit of the True Mind

inline.s: Someone says: When one cultivates the cause with a mind, there is no doubt that merit will follow. When one cultivates the cause without a mind, whence does merit come? I answer: To cultivate the cause with a mind is to obtain an effect in the realm of the conditioned; to take as cause the mindless is to reveal the merit of the nature. These manifold merits are originally complete in and of themselves, but are hidden by delusion and so do not appear. Now that the delusion is removed, the merit appears. Therefore Yongjia says: 'The three bodies and four wisdoms are complete within the essence; the eight liberations and six supernormal powers are the seal of the mind-ground.' This is the merit of the nature that is inherently present within the essence. An ancient verse says: 'If a person sits in stillness for a single moment, it surpasses raising countless javan jeweled stupas; the jeweled stupa will in the end turn to dust, while a single thought of pure mind attains right enlightenment.' From this we know that the mindless has greater merit than the mindful.

Question: When one cultivates the cause with a mind, naturally there will be merit. When one cultivates the cause without a mind, whence does merit come? Answer: To cultivate the cause with a mind is to obtain an effect in the realm of the conditioned; to take as cause the mindless is to reveal the merit of the self-nature. These manifold merits are originally complete in and of themselves, but because they are covered over by the deluded mind they do not appear. Now that the deluded mind is removed, the merit appears. Therefore Master Yongjia says in his Song of Realizing the Way: 'The three bodies and four wisdoms are complete within the essence; the eight liberations and six supernormal powers are the seal of the mind-ground.' This is the merit of the self-nature inherently present within the wondrous essence of the true mind. An ancient verse says: 'If a person sits in stillness for a single moment, it surpasses raising countless javan jeweled stupas; the jeweled stupa will in the end turn to dust, while a single thought of pure mind attains right enlightenment.' From this we know that cultivating the cause with a mindless state has greater merit than cultivating the cause with a mind.

a single thought of pure mind attains right enlightenment” — to unify one's thought in order to purify one's mind, and so cultivate right enlightenment (the Buddha-fruit). The word “one” in this phrase is a verb and not a numeral; the meaning of “single thought” is: to make one's thought one — to unify one's thought.

[The three bodies] the Dharma-body, the Reward-body, and the Response-body. The Dharma-body is also called the self-nature body, or the Dharma-nature body, that is, the true nature that is ever-abiding and unperishing and that every person possesses, except that we sentient beings are deluded and therefore it is not revealed, whereas the Buddha is awakened and has realized it. The Reward-body is formed from the Buddha's wisdom and merit, and is distinguished as the reward-body of self-enjoyment and the reward-body for the enjoyment of others; the reward-body of self-enjoyment is the body by which the Buddha enjoys the bliss of the inner realization of the Dharma, while the reward-body for the enjoyment of others is the body that the Buddha manifests to preach the Dharma to the bodhisattvas of the ten grounds. The Response-body is also called the response-transformation body, or the transformation body, that is, the Buddha-body manifested in response to the capacities and conditions of sentient beings. [The four wisdoms] the four kinds of wisdom of the Tathagata: the wisdom of accomplished action, the wisdom of wondrous contemplation, the wisdom of equality, and the wisdom of the great perfect mirror. The wisdom of accomplished action is formed by transforming the conditioned first five consciousnesses, and is the Buddha's wisdom for accomplishing everything that universally benefits sentient beings. The wisdom of wondrous contemplation is formed by transforming the conditioned sixth consciousness, and is the Buddha's wisdom for observing all dharmas and the capacities of all sentient beings and, prescribing medicine according to the illness, converting the ordinary into the sagely. The wisdom of equality is formed by transforming the conditioned seventh consciousness, and is the Buddha's wisdom whereby, being fully aware of the principle of selflessness and equality, he brings forth unconditional great compassion toward all sentient beings. The wisdom of the great perfect mirror is formed by transforming the conditioned eighth consciousness, and is the Buddha's wisdom for clearly and fully reflecting upon all phenomenal marks and principles; this wisdom is pure, perfect, and bright, seeing clearly within and without, like a great perfect mirror that illuminates all things.

[The eight liberations] these are the eight liberations, eight kinds of meditative concentration that train one in removing craving and attachment. First, having the notion of form within, one contemplates forms outside and is liberated: this means that if within the mind there is the notion of form (physical matter), it will give rise to greed; one should contemplate the manifold impurities outside so that greed has no way to arise, hence it is called liberation. Second, without the notion of form within, one contemplates forms outside and is liberated: this means that although in the mind there is no greedy thought of form, in order to make the resolve not to give rise to greed even firmer, one must still contemplate the manifold impurities outside so that greed can never arise, hence it is called liberation. Third, the pure liberation of the body as realization abiding in fullness: that is, single-mindedly contemplating the luminous, pure, wondrous, jeweled form — this is called the pure liberation; when one contemplates this pure form and can avoid giving rise to greed, one is able to attest to the mind-nature as already liberated, hence it is called the body as realization; and because this contemplation is entirely perfect and complete, one can abide settled in concentration, hence it is called abiding in fullness. Fourth, the liberation of the realm of limitless space. Fifth, the liberation of the realm of limitless consciousness. Sixth, the liberation of the realm of nothing whatsoever. Seventh, the liberation of the realm of neither perception nor non-perception. (These four liberations, the fourth through the seventh, are for those practicing concentration in the formless realm; each, while practicing concentration, contemplates suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and non-self, so that the mind is willing to relinquish everything, hence they are called liberations.) Eighth, the liberation of the cessation of perception and feeling, the body as realization abiding in fullness: the concentration of the cessation of perception and feeling is also called the concentration of complete cessation; this means that if a person has the five faculties of eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body, he will receive the five objects of form, sound, smell, taste, and touch, and receiving the five objects, manifold false thoughts arise; if there is the meditative power of eliminating perception and feeling, then everything may be eliminated, hence it is called the concentration of complete cessation. [The six supernormal powers] six kinds of spiritual power: the celestial eye, the celestial ear, knowledge of others' minds, knowledge of past lives, the power of psychic travel, and the extinction of outflows.

The monk Shuǐlǎo of Hongzhou came to consult Mazu, asking: 'What is the meaning of the coming from the West?' He was knocked down by one kick from Mazu and suddenly awakened. Rising, he clapped his hands and roared with laughter, saying: 'How marvelous! How marvelous! The hundreds and thousands of samādhis, the measureless profound meanings — at the tip of a single hair, one instantly recognizes the source.' Then he bowed and withdrew. From this we see that merit does not come from outside; it is originally complete in and of itself. The Fourth Patriarch said to Master Lǎnrǒng: 'The hundreds and thousands of Dharma-gates all return to a single square inch; merit as countless as the sands of the Ganges all rests in the source of the mind. All the doors of precepts, concentration, and wisdom, and the transformations of supernormal power, are all completely present and never separate from your mind.' According to the words of the patriarchs, the merit of the mindless is abundant indeed; but those who delight in the merit of phenomenal marks naturally do not place faith in the merit of the mindless.

The monk Shuǐlǎo of Hongzhou came to consult Mazu, asking: 'What is the meaning of the patriarch coming from the West?' He was knocked down by one kick from Mazu and suddenly awakened. Rising, he clapped his hands and roared with laughter, saying: 'How marvelous! How marvelous! The hundreds and thousands of samādhis, the measureless profound meanings — at the tip of a single hair, one instantly recognizes the source.' Then he bowed and withdrew. From this we see that merit does not come from outside; it is originally complete in and of itself. The Fourth Patriarch of the Chan school, Daoxin, said to Master Lǎnrǒng: 'The hundreds and thousands of Dharma-gates all return to a single square inch (the mind); merit as countless as the sands of the Ganges all rests in the source of the mind. All the doors of precepts, concentration, and wisdom, and the transformations of supernormal power, are all completely present and never separate from your mind.' According to the instruction of the patriarchs, the merit of the mindless is abundant indeed; but those who delight in the merit of phenomenal marks naturally place no faith in the merit of the mindless.

[What is the meaning of the patriarch coming from the West] The first patriarch of the Chan school, Bodhidharma, came from the West to this land to transmit the Dharma — what is his essential purport? [The tip of a single hair] refers to a very small amount, a very small object, or a very small place. The Buddha Treasury Sutra says: 'Shariputra, suppose a jar of honey were set at a crossroads, and one were to say: if a person can eat the tip of a single hair of it, he will never grow old or die.' The Extensive Record of Chan Master Yunmen Kuangzhen says: 'The master entered the hall and said: If I take up a single phrase and bid you accept it directly, this is already to defecate on your head. Even if you pick up the tip of a single hair and in an instant clearly understand the whole great earth, this is still to carve a wound in one's own flesh. Even so, one must actually arrive at this state before it is so.'

blocks.text: 13. Testing the Merit of the True Mind

inline.s: Someone says: When the true mind manifests, how do we know that the true mind has matured and is unobstructed? I answer: When a person who studies the Way has obtained the manifestation of the true mind, but his habitual tendencies are not yet removed, if he encounters a familiar situation he will sometimes lose mindfulness. It is like herding an ox: although it has been trained to the point where it obeys the pull and the halter, one still does not dare to let go of the whip and rope; only when the ox's mind has been tuned and its steps are steady, and it can be driven into the crops without harming them, does one dare to slacken one's hold. At this point one no longer needs the herdboy's whip and rope, and naturally it will not harm the crops.

Question: When the true mind manifests, how do we know that the true mind has matured and is unobstructed? Answer: When a person who studies the Way has obtained the manifestation of the true mind, but because his habitual tendencies are not yet removed, if he encounters a familiar sensory realm, he will sometimes lose mindfulness. This is just like herding an ox: although it has already been trained to the point where it obeys the pull and the halter at will, one still does not dare to let go of the whip and rope; one waits until the ox's mind has been tuned and its steps are steady, and it can be driven into the field of crops without harming them, only then does one dare to let go and not use the whip and rope. At this point, the herdboy no longer needs the whip and rope, and the ox naturally will not harm the crops.

When a practitioner has obtained the true mind, he should first apply effort to nourish and preserve it, and only when he has great power and function can he benefit living beings. If one wishes to test this true mind, first take the objects he has loved throughout his life and constantly bring them before the mind. If, as before, thoughts of aversion and love arise, then the mind of the Way is not yet mature; if thoughts of aversion and love do not arise, then the mind of the Way is mature. Although it is thus mature, it is still not yet the natural state in which aversion and love no longer arise.

If a practitioner has obtained the true mind, he should first apply effort to nourish and preserve it, and only when he has great power and function can he benefit sentient beings. If one wishes to test the true mind, first take the familiar sensory realms of his whole life that readily give rise to aversion and love and constantly bring them before the mind. If, as before, thoughts of aversion and love arise, then the mind of the Way is not yet mature; if thoughts of aversion and love do not arise, then the mind of the Way is mature. Although the mind of the Way is thus mature, it is still not yet the natural state in which aversion and love no longer arise.

Again, test the mind further: if, when encountering a state of aversion and love, one deliberately brings up thoughts of aversion and love so as to take hold of the realm of aversion and love, and the mind does not rise, then this mind is unobstructed, like a white ox in the open field that does not harm the crops. In ancient times there were those who reviled the Buddha and cursed the patriarchs — such persons were in accord with this mind. Now I see those who, having only just entered the school without knowing the distance of the Way, go about reviling the Buddha and cursing the patriarchs. That is counting one's chickens too early.

Test the mind further: if, when encountering a realm of aversion and love, one deliberately brings up thoughts of aversion and love so as to take hold of the realm of aversion and love, and the thoughts of aversion and love do not arise, then this mind is already unobstructed with regard to the realm, like a white ox in the open field that does not harm the crops. In ancient times there were those who reviled the Buddha and cursed the patriarchs — such persons were in accord with this mind (the mind like a white ox in the open field). But now we see those who, having only just entered the school without yet knowing the distance of the path of meditation, go about reviling the Buddha and cursing the patriarchs. This is far too reckless!

[White ox in the open field] In Chan, this refers to the pure state that is without the slightest defilement of affliction — the white ox in the open field. Open field means the open ground outside the gate, a metaphor for a place of peace and safety; white ox indicates the pure ox of the mind. In the Ox-Herding Pictures, the ox of the mind is at first entirely black, and in the process of taming and herding it gradually turns white, until it is wholly white. [Reviling the Buddha and cursing the patriarchs] When the patriarchs revile the Buddha and curse the patriarchs, they are trying to rouse students to the point that 'all marks are false.' Even the scriptures and Buddha-images, whether sagely or worthy, once they have fallen into traces and forms, all belong to birth and death and are not the Way of reality. [Counting too early] reckoning too soon.

blocks.text: 14. The True Mind Is without Knowing

inline.s: the true mind is without knowing,” means that the true mind does not possess that kind of knowing by way of seeing, hearing, perceiving, and knowing that the deluded mind has; rather it is a numinous awareness that is without thought and without marks.

Someone says: When the true mind and the deluded mind face an object, how do we distinguish the true from the deluded? I answer: The deluded mind, in facing objects, has knowing, and because of this knowing it gives rise to greed toward agreeable objects and aversion toward disagreeable objects, and, moreover, gives rise to delusion toward neutral objects. Since it gives rise to the three poisons of greed, aversion, and delusion in the face of objects, this is clearly enough to show it is the deluded mind. A patriarch says: 'The contention of favorable and unfavorable is the sickness of the mind.' From this we know that whatever regards things as acceptable or unacceptable is the deluded mind.

Question: When the true mind and the deluded mind face an object, how do we distinguish the true from the deluded? Answer: The deluded mind, in facing objects, has knowing; knowing an agreeable object it gives rise to greed, knowing a disagreeable object it gives rise to aversion, and by permitting the mind to arise in the face of objects, this is delusion. Since it gives rise to the three poisons of greed, aversion, and delusion in the face of objects, it is clearly enough to show this is the deluded mind. A patriarch says: 'The contention of favorable and unfavorable is the sickness of the mind.' From this we know that whatever has 'acceptable' (agreeable) and 'unacceptable' (disagreeable) toward sensory realms is the deluded mind.

If it is the true mind, it is knowing without knowing. With an even mind it perfectly illumines, and so it differs from plants and trees; it does not give rise to aversion and love, and so it differs from the deluded mind. That is, in facing objects it is empty and luminous, neither averse nor loving — that which is knowing without knowing is the true mind
(too)

. Therefore the Treatise of Zhao says: 'Now the mind of the sage is subtle and formless; it cannot be called existent. The more it is exercised, the more it cannot be called nonexistent. Being beyond existence, therefore it knows without knowing; being beyond nonexistence, therefore it knows without knowing. Thus nonknowing is itself knowing, and there is no way to speak of it as different — yet it differs from the mind of the sage.' Again, the deluded mind attaches to existence in the presence of existence, and attaches to nonexistence in the presence of nonexistence; it constantly dwells in the two extremes and does not know the middle way.'

If it is the true mind, then it is knowing without knowing. Because it is able to illumine perfectly with an even (undiscriminating) mind, it differs from plants and trees; because it does not give rise to aversion and love, it differs from the deluded mind. Therefore, in facing objects it is empty and luminous (numinous awareness), neither averse nor loving — it is knowing without knowing, and that is the true mind. Hence the Treatise of Zhao says: 'Now the mind of the sage is subtle and formless; it cannot be said to be existent. The more it is put to use, the more it cannot be said to be nonexistent. Being beyond existence, therefore it knows without knowing; being beyond nonexistence, therefore it knows without knowing. Thus nonknowing is itself knowing; one cannot speak of it as existent or nonexistent (there is no way to call it different), and yet it differs from the mind of the sage.' Again, the deluded mind attaches to existence in the presence of existence and attaches to nonexistence in the presence of nonexistence; it constantly dwells in the two extremes of existence and nonexistence and does not know the middle way.

[There is no way to speak of it as different, and yet it differs from the mind of the sage] The meaning of this sentence is: if one speaks of it as existent or nonexistent, then that becomes a deluded mind that differs from the mind of the sage. For the middle way in which existence and nonexistence are utterly merged is the mind of the sage, whereas speaking of it as existent or nonexistent is the deluded mind attached to the two extremes.

Yongjia says: 'To forsake the deluded mind and take up true principle — the mind that takes and forsakes becomes a crafty falsity. The student who does not understand and practices with it deeply comes to mistake a thief for his own son.' If it is the true mind, it dwells in existence and nonexistence without falling into either, and constantly abides in the middle way. Therefore a patriarch says: 'Do not chase after conditioned things, do not abide in the patience of emptiness; with a single even mind, all things are naturally extinguished.'

Master Yongjia says in his Song of Realizing the Way: 'To forsake the deluded mind and take up true principle — the mind that takes and forsakes becomes a crafty falsity. The student who does not understand this principle and yet practices with it (the student who does not understand this principle and still uses it to practice) deeply comes to mistake a thief for his own son.' If it is the true mind, it dwells in existence and nonexistence without falling into either, and constantly abides in the middle way. Hence the third patriarch of the Chan school, Master Sengcan, says in his Song of Trusting the Mind: 'Do not chase after conditioned things, do not abide in the patience of emptiness; with a single even mind (free of aversion, love, taking, and forsaking), all things are naturally extinguished.'

The Treatise of Zhao says: 'Therefore the sage dwells in existence without being attached to existence, abides in nonexistence without being attached to nonexistence; though he does not grasp at existence or nonexistence, yet he does not abandon existence or nonexistence. Therefore he blends his light among the dust and toil, moves through the five destinies, going away in stillness,'
(po)

and coming in quiet ease, serene and nonacting, yet doing all things.' This speaks of the sage reaching out a hand to help others, moving through the five destinies to receive and transform sentient beings, though he comes and goes without any mark of coming or going. The deluded mind is not like this, so the true mind and the deluded mind are different.

The Treatise of Zhao says: 'Therefore the sage dwells in existence without being attached to existence, abides in nonexistence without being attached to nonexistence; though he does not grasp at existence or nonexistence, yet he does not abandon existence or nonexistence. Therefore he blends his light and enters the dust and toil (the world), moves through the five destinies, going away in stillness and coming in quiet ease, serene and nonacting, yet doing all things.' This speaks of the sage's skillful saving of others (reaching out a hand to help others), moving through the five destinies to receive and transform sentient beings, though he comes and goes without any mark of coming or going. The deluded mind is not like this, so the true mind and the deluded mind are different.

[Blending his light among the dust and toil] to conceal (the light of bodhi-wisdom) and enter into the dust and toil (the world). The phrase 'dust and toil' means the mind wearied by the dust of the senses, and is commonly used as a name for affliction. But in the phrase 'blending his light among the dust and toil,' it refers to the mundane world. [Blending the light and mingling with the dust] comes from Laozi's words 'to blend one's light and mingle with its dust,' meaning to unite with the dusty world without setting oneself apart. In Buddhism, it means that the Buddhas and bodhisattvas, in order to save sentient beings, must conceal the light of bodhi-wisdom and, through the skillful means of a response-transformation body, be born into a dusty world full of affliction, form ties with sentient beings, and step by step lead them into the Dharma. [The five destinies] also called the five paths, namely: hell, hungry ghosts, animals, humans, and devas. [Going in stillness and coming in quiet ease] it should probably read 'coming in quiet ease (coming peacefully).' The Commentary on the Vimalakirti Sutra says: 'Zhao says: going away in stillness, coming in quiet ease. Emerging from the dark and entering the profound — who can discern its movement?' [Reaching out a hand] The school uses this to describe the teacher who assesses the capacities of students and specifically uses the second meaning-gate as a skillful means to receive and guide them, just as parents lower their hands to caress an infant. [The second meaning-gate] the teaching and Dharma-gate of turning back from the upward equanimity into the downward realm of distinctions. In the school, the first meaning-gate (the upward gate) refers to the ultimate purport of the Buddha-way in the true and absolute state of enlightenment, or the Way of practice seeking bodhi above while not clinging to worldly conditions. In contrast, the teaching gate that is expedient and skillful, established through borrowed words and phrases, or the bodhisattva conduct that accords with worldly conditions to transform sentient beings, belongs to the second meaning-gate (the downward gate).
Question: What is the one upward path?

Answer: This refers to the true and great Way in which words are exhausted and thought is cut off, and is synonymous with 'the one upward advance.' The Record of the Transmission of the Lamp says: 'The one upward path — not transmitted even by a thousand sages; the student wears out his body like an ape grasping at a shadow.' This means that the true and great Way in which words are exhausted and thought is cut off is a wondrous path not transmitted even by a thousand sages; it is what Shakyamuni did not speak, and what Bodhidharma did not transmit; it is not uttered by the mouth, and requires no thinking. It is the supreme and most true Way that transcends words and thought, and is realized and known by oneself. Because it transcends words and thought, and returns to the source, coming to rest in the serene essence of true thusness, it is called 'the one upward path.'
[Not transmitted even by a thousand sages] that which a thousand sages cannot transmit, because it has already transcended words and thought and can only be realized and known by oneself.

Master Yuanwu Foguo said: 'The great Way has no facing or backing; the ultimate truth is beyond words entirely. It towers far above the three vehicles and rises high beyond the ten grounds; where the ten thousand dharmas cannot reach, there a special radiance arises. Before the Buddha had yet appeared, the numinous source shone alone. It does not fall within what is heard or seen, and does not follow form and sound. Directly cutting away, not a single hair's breadth; across the realm it fully displays the wondrous. Even if one gains realization on the point of a staff or takes it up under a shout, this is still a roundabout accommodation. Now if one goes further and forgets both light and states, and accords with the mind of equality, in the end this too is not the true purport. Therefore it is said: "The one upward path — not transmitted even by a thousand sages; the student wears out his body like an ape grasping at a shadow."' When one arrives here (the finest thought is stilled), principle is exhausted, phenomena are exhausted, practice is exhausted, illumination is exhausted, function is exhausted, expedience is exhausted, reality is exhausted — directly like a heaven-piercing long sword, awe-inspiring in its majestic power, like the mechanism of an iron ox that no cage can contain. Today, fortunate to face a person of clear eyes, I dare not conceal or cover it up (I dare not hide it); the eight characters are laid wide open. Raising the whisk, he said: Do you yet fully know it? Radiant through the ages, alive and vivid, the whole body is revealed throughout the great chiliocosm.' (From the Record of Chan Master Yuanwu Foguo)
[Towering above (
jiǒng
)] to rise high above. [Even if] even though. [Finer thought] the fine arising, ceasing, and flowing of the conscious mind, which is the mark of the alaya consciousness. See the article
“The Mind, Self-Nature, and Tathagatagarbha”

for details. [Eight characters] namely the eight characters of the Snow Mountain: 'What is born and ceases is extinguished; quiescent extinction is bliss.' The Mahaparinirvana Sutra says: 'All conditioned things are impermanent — this is the Dharma of arising and ceasing; when arising and ceasing has ceased, quiescent extinction is joy.' (See the article
“A Commentary on the Snow Mountain Verse”
for details.) [To know in full] to know thoroughly.

Again, the true mind is the ordinary mind, and the deluded mind is the extraordinary mind. Someone says: What is called the ordinary mind? I answer: Every person possesses a point of numinous brightness, pure as empty space, pervading all places. Toward mundane affairs it is provisionally named the nature of principle; toward deluded consciousness it is provisionally called the true mind. Without the slightest discrimination, it is not confused when meeting conditions; without a single thought of taking or forsaking, it fully meets all things. It does not chase after the shifting of the ten thousand states; even if it follows the stream and obtains the wonder, it does not depart from the pure stillness of the present place; seek it and you will know that it cannot be seen — this is the true mind.

Again, the true mind is the ordinary mind, and the deluded mind is the extraordinary mind. Question: What is the ordinary mind? Answer: Every person possesses a point of numinous brightness, pure as empty space, pervading all places. Relative to mundane affairs, it is provisionally named the nature of principle; relative to deluded consciousness, it is provisionally called the true mind. Without the slightest discrimination, it is not confused when meeting conditions; without a single thought of taking or forsaking, it fully meets all things (able to attend to everything). It does not chase after the shifting of the ten thousand states, yet it can follow the stream and obtain the wonder; it does not depart from the pure stillness of the present place — seek it and you will know that it cannot be seen; this is the true mind. (This says that the ordinary mind is the true mind.)
[The ordinary mind] the mind that is without calculation and deliberation.

Someone says: What is called the extraordinary mind? I answer: Realms have the sacred and the ordinary, realms have the defiled and the pure, realms have the annihilated and the eternal, realms have principle and phenomena, realms have birth and death, realms have motion and stillness, realms have going and coming, realms have the good and the ugly, realms have the wholesome and the unwholesome, realms have cause and effect. If one discusses them in detail, there are ten thousand differences and a thousand distinctions; here we have merely raised ten pairs, all of which are called extraordinary realms. The mind that arises following these extraordinary realms and ceases following these extraordinary realms — this mind of extraordinary realms, in contrast to the aforementioned ordinary true mind, is therefore called the extraordinary deluded mind. The true mind is inherently complete and does not follow the extraordinary realms in producing all manner of distinctions, so it is called the ordinary true mind.

Question: What is the extraordinary mind? Answer: Realms have the sacred and the ordinary, realms have the defiled and the pure, realms have the annihilated and the eternal, realms have principle and phenomena, realms have birth and death, realms have motion and stillness, realms have going and coming, realms have the good and the ugly, realms have the wholesome and the unwholesome, realms have cause and effect — these are all extraordinary realms. If one discusses the extraordinary realms in detail, there are ten thousand differences and a thousand distinctions; above I have merely raised ten pairs, all of which are called extraordinary realms (realms with dualistic opposition). If the mind arises following these extraordinary realms and ceases following these extraordinary realms, then this mind of arising and ceasing that follows the extraordinary realms, in contrast to the aforementioned ordinary true mind, is called the extraordinary deluded mind. The true mind is inherently complete and does not follow the extraordinary realms in producing all manner of distinctions, so it is called the ordinary true mind.

Someone says: The true mind is ordinary and has no various differing causes. How is it, then, that the Buddha speaks of cause and effect, of good and evil, and of retribution? I answer: The deluded mind pursues all manner of realms, and not understanding all manner of realms, it thereupon gives rise to all manner of minds. The Buddha speaks of all manner of dharmas of cause and effect in order to subdue all manner of deluded minds, and so cause and effect must be established. If this true mind did not pursue all manner of realms, and so did not give rise to all manner of minds, then the Buddha would not speak all manner of dharmas — how could there be cause and effect?

Question: The true mind is ordinary and has no dualistic opposition (no various differing causes). Why, then, does the Buddha speak of cause and effect, of good and evil, and of retribution? Answer: The deluded mind pursues all manner of realms and, not understanding the reality of all manner of realms, it thereupon gives rise to all manner of minds. The Buddha speaks of all manner of dharmas of cause and effect in order to subdue all manner of deluded minds, so cause and effect must be established. If this true mind did not pursue all manner of realms, and so did not give rise to all manner of minds, then the Buddha would not speak all manner of dharmas — how could there then be any talk of cause and effect, of good and evil, and of retribution?

Someone says: Does the ordinary true mind never give rise to mind at all? I answer: The true mind sometimes functions and gives rise to mind, but not following from realms; it is only a wondrous function at play, not unmindful of cause and effect.'

Question: Does the true mind then never give rise to mind? Answer: The true mind sometimes functions and gives rise to mind, but it does not give rise following from realms (it gives rise to a mind that abides nowhere); it is only a wondrous function at play, not unmindful of cause and effect.
[The true mind sometimes functions but does not arise following from realms] This is exactly the meaning of 'one should give rise to the mind that abides nowhere' in the Diamond Sutra. (See
“A Detailed Explanation of the Diamond Sutra”
Question: Does the true mind know, or is it without knowing?
Answer: It knows. The Shurangama Sutra says:
Establishing knowledge upon knowledge and views — this is the root of ignorance.'

This shows that before ignorance had arisen there was originally knowing, and this is the knowing of the true mind. This knowing is the knowing of prajna. And the knowledge that is established is the seeing, hearing, perceiving, and knowing of the deluded mind, which is the shadow of conditions upon the six sense-objects. The Shurangama Sutra goes on to say:
“Knowledge and views, without views — this is nirvana.'
This knowing that is without views is the knowing of the true mind. Master Hanshan says in his Record of Contemplating the Lankavatara:
When the mind is still and knows, both true and false are abandoned — this is called the noble wisdom of self-awakening.'
And Master Yongjia says in the fourth hymn on Shamatha of his
Collected Writings on the Chan School from Yongjia:
After forgetting conditions, still and quiet, the numinous knowing-nature
(the essence of mind)
nowhere trembling is luminous.'
Sengzhao says in his Treatise on Prajna Being without Knowing:

Because the mind of the sage is without knowing, therefore it knows all things. The knowing of not-knowing is called the knowing of all. Therefore the sutra says: 'The mind of the sage knows nothing yet knows all.' It is so indeed!'
Question: The single word 'know' has long been a matter of debate. Master Guifeng says:
“The one word 'know' is the gate of all wonders.'
Chan Master Sixin of Huanglong says:
“The one word 'know' is the gate of all calamities.'
May I ask, which is right?
Answer: The Shurangama Sutra says:
“Establishing knowledge upon knowledge and views — this is the root of ignorance.'

The first 'know' in the sentence is the gate of all wonders; if one sinks into the second 'know,' then one is a sick eye seeing flowers in the sky, and moreover inviting those flowers to yield empty fruit — this is the gate of all calamities. Master Hanshan says:

“Before the Buddha came forth, before the patriarch came from the West, there is a ready-made inheritance that every person fully possesses. Because one possesses it fully yet does not know it, therefore the Yellow-faced
(Shakyamuni Buddha)
and the Blue-eyed
(Patriarch Bodhidharma)
could not help coming forth in person to explain it for people. The hundred myriad on Vulture Peak, and the seventeen hundred lamp-transmissions
(the seventeen hundred gong'an of the Record of the Transmission of the Lamp and the like)

, all turned back at a single call and at once knew what had been inherently theirs. This is 'the one word "know" is the gate of all wonders.' Alas! The Buddhas and patriarchs originally have no real Dharma to hand over to people — how could they have expected that every person's sick eye sees flowers in the sky and then invites the flowers to bear fruit? Is this truly the mind of the Buddhas and patriarchs? This is 'the one word "know" is the gate of all calamities.' If we do not carefully scrape again with the golden pick
(removing the film over the eye, so that a sick eye may not see flowers in the sky)
, how are we to inherit
(inherit and shoulder)
that inheritance?'
(From the Collection of Dream Wandering
the Preface on Sending Master Wuyan to Preside at Shaolin.) Master Zibo (Citrine) said:
“The one word 'know' is the gate of all wonders; to establish knowledge upon knowledge and views, the calamity is great indeed.'
(From the Collected Writings of Master Citrine)
[The one word 'know' is the gate of all wonders] Master Guifeng says in the General Preface to the Collection of Explanations of the Sources of Chan:

All dharmas are like a dream, as all the sages agree. Therefore the deluded thought is originally still, and the sense-dust realms are originally empty. The empty and still mind is a numinous awareness that is never dimmed. This very empty and still awareness is your true nature. Whether deluded or awakened, the mind originally knows by itself; it is not born depending on conditions, and does not arise because of objects. The one word 'know' is the gate of all wonders. Because of beginningless delusion, one falsely grasps body and mind as self, giving rise to thoughts of greed, aversion, and so on. If one obtains the guidance of a good friend and at once awakens to this empty and still awareness — and awareness is without thought and without form — who is there to be a mark of self or a mark of person? Perceiving that all marks are empty, the mind is naturally without thought.'
When a thought arises, one at once becomes aware; being aware of it, it is gone — the wondrous gate of practice lies solely in this.

Therefore though one practices all the myriad practices, one takes the absence of thought as the principle. If one attains the understanding of the absence of thought, then love and aversion are naturally softened, compassion and wisdom naturally grow bright, offenses naturally are eradicated, and merit and practice naturally advance. Having understood that all marks are not marks, there is naturally the cultivation that is non-cultivation. When affliction is exhausted, birth and death are immediately cut off. When what is born-and-ceasing has ceased, still illumination appears before one, functioning without limit — this is called Buddha.

[Unable to contain a laugh] unable to keep from laughing. 'To contain a laugh' means to hold in a smile; 'unable to contain' means unable to control oneself. [To scrape again with the golden pick] to remove the film over the eye, so that a sick eye may not see flowers in the sky. A verse says: 'the confused film over the eye is scraped by the golden pick.' [The golden pick] a tool used in ancient times to treat eye disease. Its shape resembles an arrowhead, and it is used to scrape the film of the eye.
